items.title: South Africa: the laboratory of Satyagraha (1893-1914)
items.body:
### South Africa — where Satyagraha was born

**In one line**
Gandhi spent 1893-1914 in South Africa fighting racial discrimination against Indians, and it was there that he invented his method of non-violent resistance, Satyagraha.

**Why it is asked**
The exam treats South Africa as the 'rehearsal' for India, so it tests the body Gandhi founded, the newspaper he ran, and the specific laws he fought.

**The story**
Gandhi (born **2 October 1869** at Porbandar, Gujarat) studied law in England and sailed to **South Africa in 1893** for the **Dada Abdulla** commercial case. Shocked by the treatment of Indians, he stayed until **1914**. His struggle had two phases: a **moderate phase (1894-1906)** of petitions and memorials, and a **passive-resistance / Satyagraha phase (1906-1914)** of open but non-violent defiance. He founded the **Natal Indian Congress** to unite Indians and started the newspaper **Indian Opinion** to spread his ideas. His campaigns opposed **compulsory registration certificates** (which carried fingerprints and were publicly burned), the **£3 poll tax** on ex-indentured labourers, a court ruling that **invalidated non-Christian marriages**, and the **Transvaal Immigration Act**. The reformer **Gopal Krishna Gokhale** visited and mobilised Indian opinion, and a negotiated settlement ended the campaign — giving Gandhi the confidence to apply Satyagraha at home.

**Picture it**

| Grievance | Gandhi's response |
|---|---|
| Compulsory registration certificates (fingerprints) | Passive Resistance Association; certificates publicly burned |
| Restrictions on Indian migration | Defied by crossing provinces without licences |
| £3 poll tax; invalidation of non-Christian marriages | Combined mass campaign |
| Transvaal Immigration Act | Gokhale mobilised opinion; compromise reached |

**Terms explained**
- **Satyagraha** — literally 'holding firmly to truth': non-violent resistance based on Truth and Non-violence.
- **Indentured labour** — workers bound by contract to serve for years, often in harsh conditions overseas.
- **Poll tax** — a flat tax per person; here £3 charged on ex-indentured Indians to force them to re-indenture or leave.
- **Natal Indian Congress** — the organisation Gandhi set up in 1894 to represent Indians in Natal.

**Don't confuse**
- **Natal Indian Congress (South Africa)** with the **Indian National Congress (India)** — different bodies.
- The **moderate phase (petitions)** with the **Satyagraha phase (civil defiance)** — both happened in South Africa.

**Remember it**
South Africa = Gandhi's 'laboratory' — he tested Satyagraha abroad before using it in India.

**TL;DR**
- Gandhi born 2 October 1869 at Porbandar; studied law in England.
- In South Africa 1893-1914 (Dada Abdulla case); founded the Natal Indian Congress and Indian Opinion.
- Satyagraha, resting on Truth and Non-violence, was first developed here.
- Campaigns fought registration certificates, the £3 poll tax and the invalidation of non-Christian marriages.
keyPoints: Gandhi born 2 October 1869 at Porbandar, Gujarat; studied law in England.
Went to South Africa in 1893 (Dada Abdulla case); stayed till 1914.
Founded the Natal Indian Congress and started the newspaper 'Indian Opinion'.
Satyagraha first experimented in South Africa, resting on Truth and Non-violence.
Campaigns targeted registration certificates, the £3 poll tax and invalidation of non-Christian marriages.

items.title: The three early Indian Satyagrahas (1917-1918)
items.body:
### Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda

**In one line**
In his first three Indian campaigns Gandhi proved that non-violent resistance could win real victories, and each is remembered as a 'first' of its kind.

**Why it is asked**
The exam constantly matches these three to their cause, year and 'first' tag, and mixes up which one involved the fast and which the no-tax demand.

**The story**
Gandhi returned to India in **1915**; on his guru **Gopal Krishna Gokhale's** advice he first spent a year touring the country to understand its people. His first struggle was the **Champaran Satyagraha (1917)** in Bihar, defending peasants forced to grow indigo under the **Tin-Kathia system** — the first civil-disobedience-type act, supported by Rajendra Prasad and J.B. Kripalani. Next came the **Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918)**, a dispute over the withdrawn plague bonus, in which Gandhi undertook his **first fast-unto-death** and the social worker **Anasuya Sarabhai** helped the workers; they demanded a 50% rise and settled for a 35% bonus. Then the **Kheda Satyagraha (1918)** in Gujarat was the **first no-tax campaign**: when drought ruined crops but the government refused to remit revenue, Gandhi led resistance and **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** rose as a leader.

**Picture it**

| Satyagraha | Year | Cause | 'First' tag | Associates |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Champaran | 1917 | Forced indigo (Tin-Kathia), Bihar | First civil-disobedience-type act | Rajendra Prasad, Kripalani |
| Ahmedabad Mill Strike | 1918 | Withdrawal of plague bonus | Gandhi's first fast-unto-death | Anasuya Sarabhai |
| Kheda | 1918 | Revenue not remitted despite drought | First no-tax campaign | Sardar Patel |

**Terms explained**
- **Tin-Kathia** — the rule forcing peasants to grow indigo on 3 of every 20 kathas per bigha of land.
- **Fast-unto-death** — a hunger strike continued until the demand is met (or the faster dies).
- **No-tax campaign** — a refusal to pay land revenue as a form of protest.
- **Remission** — official cancellation or reduction of tax, owed here because the crop failed.

**Don't confuse**
- **Champaran (indigo, Bihar)** with **Kheda (revenue, Gujarat)** — different grievances and states.
- **Ahmedabad (the fast)** with **Kheda (the no-tax demand)** — both 1918, different 'firsts'.

**Remember it**
Cham-**paran** = **p**easants/indigo; Ahmeda-**bad** = **b**onus/fast; **Kh**eda = no-tax (Patel).

**TL;DR**
- Gandhi arrived in India in 1915; Gokhale was his political guru.
- Champaran (1917): first Indian Satyagraha, against indigo under Tin-Kathia.
- Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918): first fast-unto-death; Anasuya Sarabhai assisted.
- Kheda (1918): first no-tax campaign; Sardar Patel emerged.
keyPoints: Gandhi arrived in India in 1915; Gopal Krishna Gokhale was his political guru.
Champaran (1917): first Indian Satyagraha, against indigo under the Tin-Kathia system.
Ahmedabad Mill Strike (1918): Gandhi's first fast-unto-death; Anasuya Sarabhai assisted workers.
Kheda (1918): first no-tax Satyagraha; Sardar Patel emerged as a leader.
These local wins made Gandhi the undisputed leader of the freedom struggle.

items.title: Gandhi's three great mass movements
items.body:
### Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India

**In one line**
Gandhi led three nationwide movements — Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience and Quit India — that turned the Congress into a movement of millions.

**Why it is asked**
These three are the backbone of the Gandhian era; the exam tests their dates, methods, why Gandhi launched each, and why Non-Cooperation was called off.

**The story**
The **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22)** was India's **first mass movement**. It fused three grievances: the **Punjab wrong** (the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre), the **Khilafat issue** (Muslim anger at the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph and the dismantling of the Caliphate — Gandhi backed it to protest that treatment and thereby cement **Hindu-Muslim unity**), and the demand for **Swaraj**. Its programme was boycott — of foreign goods, official titles, government schools and courts — alongside the promotion of khadi and new national institutions such as **Jamia Millia** and **Kashi Vidyapeeth**. Gandhi suddenly **withdrew it after the Chauri Chaura incident (February 1922)**, when a mob burnt a police station, because it broke his rule of non-violence. The **Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34)** opened with the famous **Dandi Salt March (12 March to 6 April 1930)**, breaking the salt law. The **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** paused it and took Gandhi to the **Second Round Table Conference** — the only one he attended. Finally, the **Quit India Movement (1942)** was launched with the cry **'Do or Die'** after the Cripps Mission failed; with leaders jailed at once, it became a largely leaderless mass upsurge.

**Picture it**

| Movement | Years | Launch / method | End or turn |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-Cooperation | 1920-22 | Boycott + Khilafat + Swaraj | Withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922) |
| Civil Disobedience | 1930-34 | Dandi Salt March | Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931), 2nd RTC |
| Quit India | 1942 | 'Do or Die' | Leaders jailed; mass upsurge |

**Terms explained**
- **Non-Cooperation** — withdrawing all cooperation from the government by boycotting its goods, titles and institutions.
- **Khilafat** — the Muslim campaign to protect the Ottoman Caliph, which Gandhi joined for Hindu-Muslim unity.
- **Civil Disobedience** — deliberately but peacefully breaking a specific unjust law, like the salt law.
- **Round Table Conference (RTC)** — London talks (1930-32) between the British and Indian representatives on reform.

**Don't confuse**
- **Non-Cooperation (boycott of institutions, 1920)** with **Civil Disobedience (breaking laws, 1930)**.
- **Chauri Chaura (ended Non-Cooperation, 1922)** with the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (paused Civil Disobedience, 1931)**.

**Remember it**
Gandhi stops a movement on principle — Chauri Chaura's violence is exactly why he called off Non-Cooperation.

**TL;DR**
- Non-Cooperation (1920-22): first mass movement; Punjab + Khilafat + Swaraj; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922).
- Rowlatt Act (1919) was a 'Black Act'; Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919) under General Reginald Dyer.
- Civil Disobedience began with the Dandi Salt March, 1930.
- Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) took Gandhi to the Second (and only) Round Table Conference he attended.
- Quit India (August 1942) was launched with 'Do or Die'.
keyPoints: Non-Cooperation (1920-22): first mass movement; combined Punjab, Khilafat and Swaraj; withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (1922).
Rowlatt Act (1919) was condemned as a 'Black Act'; Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 Apr 1919) under Gen. Dyer followed.
Civil Disobedience began with the Dandi Salt March, 1930.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) took Gandhi to the Second Round Table Conference — the only RTC he attended.
Quit India (Aug 1942) was launched with the slogan 'Do or Die'.

items.title: Gandhian thought: Satyagraha, trusteeship and constructive work
items.body:
### The core of Gandhian thought

**In one line**
Gandhi's politics flowed from a few linked ideas — truth, non-violence, the unity of means and ends, trusteeship, and hands-on constructive work.

**Why it is asked**
Paper-2 and the ethics-flavoured questions test the meaning of Satyagraha, the means-ends doctrine of *Hind Swaraj*, trusteeship and the Poona Pact, so the definitions must be precise.

**The story**
**Satyagraha** ('holding to truth') stands on two pillars — **Truth (Satya)** and **Non-violence (Ahimsa)**. A Satyagrahi is truthful, fearless and ready to suffer, acting out of **love for the opponent, never hatred**; the methods are **non-cooperation and civil disobedience** — non-payment of taxes, peaceful protest and the return of honours. **Don't confuse** Satyagraha never permits violence, not even in 'just' self-defence; the Satyagrahi accepts suffering instead. In his book **Hind Swaraj (1909)** Gandhi set out the **unity of means and ends**: a pure end such as Swaraj can be reached only through pure, non-violent means, so the end never justifies impure means. His idea of **trusteeship** asked the wealthy to treat their surplus wealth as held in trust for society rather than owned absolutely. Alongside agitation he stressed a **constructive programme**: spinning khadi on the charkha, the removal of untouchability (he called the depressed classes **'Harijans'**, children of God, and set up the **All India Harijan League / Harijan Sevak Sangh, 1932**), Hindu-Muslim unity, and self-reliant village life. When the **Communal Award (1932)** granted separate electorates to the Depressed Classes, Gandhi fasted, and the resulting **Poona Pact (1932)** with **B.R. Ambedkar** replaced them with reserved seats within the general electorate.

**Picture it**

```
Truth + Non-violence → Satyagraha
        │
        ├── Means = Ends (Hind Swaraj, 1909)
        ├── Trusteeship (wealth held for society)
        └── Constructive programme (khadi · anti-untouchability · unity · villages)
```

**Terms explained**
- **Ahimsa** — non-violence in thought, word and deed; for Gandhi it was absolute, never permitting violence.
- **Trusteeship** — the idea that the rich should manage surplus wealth as trustees for the whole community.
- **Harijan** — Gandhi's term ('children of God') for the depressed classes, in his anti-untouchability work.
- **Communal Award** — Ramsay MacDonald's 1932 scheme giving separate electorates, including to the Depressed Classes.

**Don't confuse**
- **Separate electorates (Communal Award)** with **reserved seats (Poona Pact)** — the Pact swapped the first for the second.
- **Trusteeship (voluntary sharing by the rich)** with socialist confiscation — Gandhi rejected class violence.

**Remember it**
For Gandhi the road and the destination are the same thing — impure means can never reach a pure end.

**TL;DR**
- Satyagraha rests on Truth and Ahimsa; the Satyagrahi suffers willingly and never uses violence.
- Means-ends unity: pure ends require pure (non-violent) means (Hind Swaraj, 1909).
- Trusteeship: the rich hold surplus wealth in trust for society.
- Constructive programme: khadi/charkha, anti-untouchability (Harijan upliftment), Hindu-Muslim unity.
- Poona Pact (1932): reserved seats replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.
keyPoints: Satyagraha rests on Truth and Ahimsa; the Satyagrahi suffers willingly and never uses violence.
Means-ends unity: pure ends require pure (non-violent) means (Hind Swaraj, 1909).
Trusteeship: the rich hold surplus wealth in trust for society.
Constructive programme: khadi/charkha, anti-untouchability (Harijan upliftment), Hindu-Muslim unity.
Poona Pact (1932): reserved seats replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

items.title: Titles, martyrdom and the Andhra connection
items.body:
### Titles, death and Andhra's response

**In one line**
Gandhi became the 'Father of the Nation', led the Congress session only once, was assassinated in 1948, and his call stirred Andhra's leaders and poets.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC adds a regional layer, so it asks both the all-India facts (titles, sole presidency, assassination) and Andhra's specific contribution.

**The story**
By converting scattered local struggles into one national movement, Gandhi earned the titles **'Mahatma'** and **'Father of the Nation'**. Despite his towering role, he **presided over the Indian National Congress only once, at the Belgaum session (1924)**. He was shot dead at **Birla House, Delhi, on 30 January 1948** by **Nathuram Godse**; the day is observed as **Martyrs' Day**. In **Andhra**, the response to Gandhi was strong: **Tanguturi Prakasam** (nicknamed **'Andhra Kesari'**), **Konda Venkatappayya** and **Pattabhi Sitaramayya** led Congress work, while the nationalist poet **Garimella Satyanarayana** fired up ordinary people with patriotic songs that the British banned. Gandhi himself toured Andhra promoting khadi, and this mobilisation later fed the demand for a separate linguistic **Andhra state**.

**Picture it**

| Fact | Detail |
|---|---|
| Titles | 'Mahatma' and 'Father of the Nation' |
| Only INC presidency | Belgaum, 1924 |
| Assassination | 30 January 1948, by Nathuram Godse (Martyrs' Day) |
| Andhra leaders | Prakasam, Konda Venkatappayya, Pattabhi Sitaramayya |
| Andhra poet | Garimella Satyanarayana (songs banned) |

**Terms explained**
- **Martyrs' Day (Shaheed Diwas)** — 30 January, marking the anniversary of Gandhi's assassination.
- **Andhra Kesari** — 'Lion of Andhra', the title of Tanguturi Prakasam.
- **Linguistic state** — a state formed on the basis of a common language, as Andhra later demanded.

**Don't confuse**
- **'Mahatma' (given by Tagore)** with **'Father of the Nation' (popularised by Bose)** — two different titles and sources.
- **Tanguturi Prakasam (Andhra Kesari)** with **Pattabhi Sitaramayya (Congress historian/leader)**.

**Remember it**
Gandhi led the Congress session just once — at Belgaum, 1924 — a favourite one-mark trap.

**TL;DR**
- Titles: 'Mahatma' and 'Father of the Nation'.
- Presided over the INC only once — Belgaum session, 1924.
- Assassinated 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Godse (observed as Martyrs' Day).
- Andhra leaders: Prakasam (Andhra Kesari), Konda Venkatappayya, Pattabhi Sitaramayya; poet Garimella Satyanarayana.
keyPoints: Titles: 'Mahatma' and 'Father of the Nation'.
Presided over the INC only once — Belgaum session, 1924.
Assassinated on 30 January 1948 by Nathuram Godse (observed as Martyrs' Day).
Andhra leaders: Tanguturi Prakasam (Andhra Kesari), Konda Venkatappayya, Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
Poet Garimella Satyanarayana energised Andhra's participation in Gandhian movements.

items.title: Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Roles & Writings (PYQ set)
items.body:
### Pact, roles and writings (exam-focused)

**In one line**
These are the exact, repeatedly tested details — what the Gandhi-Irwin Pact did and did not give, Gandhi's specific roles, and his newspapers, books and titles.

**Why it is asked**
Each point below has appeared as a UPSC/APPSC question, often as a multi-statement item where one wrong detail (like a police-excess enquiry) decides the answer.

**The story**
The **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 March 1931)** had the government agree to **withdraw the ordinances issued to curb the Civil Disobedience Movement** and the prosecutions, **release political prisoners** not guilty of violence, and permit **coastal salt manufacture** for personal use; in return the Congress agreed to **suspend Civil Disobedience** and attend the **Second Round Table Conference**. Crucially it did **not** concede an **enquiry into police excesses** — a classic exam trap. On Gandhi's roles: he was **instrumental in abolishing indentured labour** emigration (ended **1917**); at the **1918 Delhi War Conference** under Chelmsford he actually **supported recruiting** Indians to the British army (so 'did not support' is false); and after the **Salt Law was broken (1930)** the government **declared the Congress illegal**. The **Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919)** targeted the **Rowlatt (Sedition Committee) Act**, and Gandhi used the existing **Home Rule League** network to spread it — his first all-India political act. His writings and papers: newspapers **Indian Opinion, Young India, Navajivan, Harijan**; books **Hind Swaraj (1909)**, the autobiography **My Experiments with Truth**, and **'Songs from Prison'** (his translation of Indian devotional lyrics). The title **'Mahatma'** was given by **Rabindranath Tagore** and **'Father of the Nation'** popularised by **Subhas Chandra Bose**; during Quit India he was detained at the **Aga Khan Palace, Pune**.

**Picture it**

| Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931) | In the Pact? |
|---|---|
| Withdraw ordinances/prosecutions | Yes |
| Release non-violent prisoners | Yes |
| Allow coastal salt for personal use | Yes |
| Enquiry into police excesses | NO (refused) |

**Terms explained**
- **Ordinance** — a law made by the executive (here, emergency measures to crush Civil Disobedience).
- **Indentured (girmitiya) labour** — contract labourers shipped overseas; the system ended in 1917.
- **Sedition Committee** — the Rowlatt Committee whose report led to the 1919 Rowlatt Act.
- **Aga Khan Palace, Pune** — the building where Gandhi was detained during Quit India (1942).

**Don't confuse**
- The Gandhi-Irwin Pact's three concessions with the **rejected** police-excess enquiry — the fourth is NOT in it.
- **'Mahatma' (Tagore)** with **'Father of the Nation' (Bose)**.
- **Hind Swaraj (a book, 1909)** with his **newspapers** (Young India, Navajivan, Harijan).

**Remember it**
Gandhi-Irwin gives **three releases** (ordinances, prisoners, salt) but **NOT** a police-excess enquiry.

**TL;DR**
- Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 Mar 1931): withdraw ordinances, release non-violent prisoners, allow coastal salt; Congress joins 2nd RTC — but NO police-excess enquiry.
- Gandhi helped end indentured labour (1917); at the 1918 War Conference he supported recruitment; after the Salt Law the INC was declared illegal.
- Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) opposed the Rowlatt/Sedition Committee Act, using the Home Rule League network.
- Newspapers: Indian Opinion, Young India, Navajivan, Harijan; books: Hind Swaraj (1909), My Experiments with Truth, 'Songs from Prison'.
- 'Mahatma' by Tagore; 'Father of the Nation' by Bose; Quit India detention at Aga Khan Palace, Pune.
keyPoints: Gandhi-Irwin Pact (5 Mar 1931): withdraw ordinances, release non-violent prisoners, allow coastal salt; Congress joins 2nd RTC — but NO enquiry into police excesses.
Gandhi was instrumental in ending indentured labour (1917); at the 1918 War Conference he supported army recruitment; after the Salt Law the INC was declared illegal.
Rowlatt Satyagraha (1919) opposed the Rowlatt/Sedition Committee Act; Gandhi used the Home Rule League network.
Newspapers: Indian Opinion, Young India, Navajivan, Harijan; books: Hind Swaraj (1909), My Experiments with Truth, 'Songs from Prison'.
'Mahatma' given by Tagore; 'Father of the Nation' by Bose; Quit India detention at Aga Khan Palace, Pune.

items.title: Gandhi's Early Life, South Africa and His Ashrams — Detail
items.body:
### Gandhi's Early Life, South Africa and His Ashrams — Detail

**In one line**
The facts of Gandhi's life up to 1915 — family, London, the train at Pietermaritzburg, the first satyagraha in 1906 and the settlement of 1914 — and the ashrams he built.

**The story**
Born at Porbandar to **Karamchand** and **Putlibai**, Gandhi married **Kasturba** in 1883 and studied law at the **Inner Temple**, London. In South Africa a guard threw him out of a first-class carriage at **Pietermaritzburg** (June 1893) — the night he decided to resist. He founded the **Natal Indian Congress** (1894) and **Indian Opinion** (1903), and served with an **Ambulance Corps** in the **Boer War**. On **11 September 1906**, at the **Empire Theatre** in Johannesburg, Indians vowed to defy the Asiatic registration law; the **Passive Resistance Association** led them. The **£3** poll tax, the **Searle** judgment (1913) and the **Great March** from **Newcastle** followed, and the Gandhi–**Smuts** agreement produced the **Indian Relief Act** (1914). He landed at Bombay on **9 January 1915**. His communities — **Phoenix** (Durban), **Tolstoy Farm** (with **Kallenbach**), **Kochrab**, **Sabarmati** (1917) and **Sevagram** near **Wardha** (1936) — were laboratories of simple living.

#### Life and South Africa

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Parents** | Father **Karamchand** (diwan of Porbandar), mother **Putlibai** |
| **Marriage** | **Kasturba**, **1883** (aged 13) |
| **Law studies** | **Inner Temple**, London, 1888–**1891**; barrister |
| **Turning point** | Thrown off a first-class carriage at **Pietermaritzburg** (7 June 1893) |
| **Natal Indian Congress** | Founded **1894** (moderate petition phase 1894–1906) |
| **Indian Opinion** | Newspaper, **1903** (English, Gujarati and other languages) |
| **War service** | Indian **Ambulance Corps** — **Boer War** 1899, Zulu rising 1906; earned the Kaiser-i-Hind medal |
| **First satyagraha** | Mass meeting at the **Empire Theatre**, Johannesburg, **11 September 1906**, against the Asiatic registration "Black Act" |
| **Passive Resistance Association** | Defied registration; certificates publicly burned (1908) |
| **Marriage issue** | **Searle** judgment, **1913** — non-Christian marriages invalid |
| **Poll tax** | **£3** a year on every ex-indentured Indian |
| **Great March** | Nov 1913, miners from **Newcastle** into the **Transvaal** |
| **Settlement** | Gandhi–**Smuts** agreement → **Indian Relief Act** 1914 (poll tax abolished, Indian marriages valid) |
| **Return to India** | **9 January 1915**, Bombay — now **Pravasi Bharatiya Divas** |

#### Ashrams and settlements

| Ashram | Year and place |
|---|---|
| **Phoenix Settlement** | **1904**, near **Durban** (after reading Ruskin) |
| **Tolstoy Farm** | **1910**, near Johannesburg, with Hermann **Kallenbach** |
| **Kochrab Ashram** | **1915**, Ahmedabad (Satyagraha Ashram) |
| **Sabarmati Ashram** | **1917**, Ahmedabad; Dandi March began here |
| **Sevagram Ashram** | **1936**, Segaon near **Wardha** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Phoenix** (1904) and **Tolstoy Farm** (1910) were in **South Africa**; **Kochrab**, **Sabarmati** and **Sevagram** in **India**.
- **9 January** (return, Pravasi Bharatiya Divas) ≠ **30 January** (death, Martyrs' Day) ≠ **2 October** (birth).

**TL;DR**
- Inner Temple, London; Pietermaritzburg, June 1893.
- Natal Indian Congress 1894; Indian Opinion 1903; first satyagraha Empire Theatre 11 Sept 1906.
- £3 poll tax; Searle judgment 1913; Gandhi–Smuts → Indian Relief Act 1914.
- Ashrams: Phoenix 1904, Tolstoy 1910, Kochrab 1915, Sabarmati 1917, Sevagram 1936.
keyPoints: Gandhi studied law at the Inner Temple, London.
The first satyagraha was resolved at the Empire Theatre, Johannesburg, on 11 September 1906.
The Gandhi–Smuts agreement led to the Indian Relief Act of 1914.
Gandhi returned to India on 9 January 1915, now Pravasi Bharatiya Divas.
Sevagram Ashram near Wardha was set up in 1936.

items.title: Influences, Writings and Key Ideas of Gandhi
items.body:
### Influences, Writings and Key Ideas of Gandhi

**In one line**
Who shaped Gandhi, what he wrote and edited, and the vocabulary of his thought — trusteeship, Sarvodaya, Gram Swaraj, Nai Talim.

**The story**
Gandhi built his thought from many sources: **Ruskin**'s **Unto This Last** (which he paraphrased as **Sarvodaya**), **Tolstoy**'s **The Kingdom of God Is Within You**, **Thoreau**'s essay on civil disobedience, the Gita, and the Jain sage **Rajchandra**; in politics his guru was **Gokhale**. He wrote **Hind Swaraj** (1909) on the ship **Kildonan Castle**, serialised his autobiography in **Navajivan**, edited **Young India** and, from 1933, **Harijan**. His ideas form a connected system — **trusteeship** for the rich, **Sarvodaya** for all, **Gram Swaraj** for villages, **Ram Rajya** as the moral state, **Nai Talim** (1937) for schools, and the **Talisman** of the poorest face.

#### Influences

| Source | What Gandhi took |
|---|---|
| **John Ruskin** | **Unto This Last** → Gandhi's Gujarati paraphrase **Sarvodaya** (welfare of all) |
| **Leo Tolstoy** | **The Kingdom of God Is Within You**; letters 1909–10 |
| **H.D. Thoreau** | Essay **Civil Disobedience** |
| **Shrimad Rajchandra** | Jain poet-jeweller; spiritual guide |
| **G.K. Gokhale** | **Political guru**; advised a year of touring India (1915) |

#### Writings and papers

| Work | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Hind Swaraj** | **1909**, Gujarati, written on the ship **Kildonan Castle**; critique of modern civilisation; means–ends |
| **Autobiography** | **My Experiments with Truth** — Gujarati *Satyana Prayogo*, serialised in **Navajivan** (1925–29) |
| **Young India** | English weekly, **1919**–1932 |
| **Navajivan** | **Gujarati** weekly (from 1919) |
| **Harijan** | From Feb **1933**; Harijan Bandhu (Gujarati), Harijan Sevak (Hindi) |
| **Satyagraha in South Africa** | Written in Yerawada jail (1920s) |
| **Songs from Prison** | Translations of Indian devotional lyrics (made in Yerawada, 1930) |
| **Constructive Programme** | Booklet, **1941** — 18 items (khadi, village industries, basic education, etc.) |
| **Other works** | Key to Health; Gita translated as **Anasaktiyoga** |

#### Key ideas

| Idea | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Trusteeship** | Surplus wealth held in trust for society |
| **Sarvodaya** | Welfare of all (from Ruskin) |
| **Gram Swaraj** | Self-sufficient, self-governing villages |
| **Ram Rajya** | Ideal just and moral polity |
| **Nai Talim** | Wardha Scheme **1937** — learning through a craft; committee chaired by **Zakir Hussain** |
| **Talisman** | 1947 — think of the **poorest** person before acting |
| **Seven social sins** | Young India 1925 — politics without principles, wealth without work, etc. |
| **Six beliefs** | Truth, non-violence, vegetarianism, **brahmacharya**, simplicity, faith |
| **Swadeshi (Gandhian)** | Neighbourhood first; **khadi** and **village industry** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Indian Opinion** (South Africa, 1903) → **Young India** & **Navajivan** (1919) → **Harijan** (1933).
- **Sarvodaya** = Gandhi's word from Ruskin; the post-1947 **Sarvodaya/Bhoodan** movement was Vinoba Bhave's.

**TL;DR**
- Influences: Ruskin (Unto This Last → Sarvodaya), Tolstoy, Thoreau, Rajchandra; political guru Gokhale.
- Hind Swaraj 1909 (Kildonan Castle); autobiography in Navajivan 1925–29; Young India 1919; Harijan 1933.
- Ideas: trusteeship, Sarvodaya, Gram Swaraj, Ram Rajya, Nai Talim 1937 (Zakir Hussain), Talisman 1947.
keyPoints: Gandhi paraphrased Ruskin's Unto This Last as Sarvodaya.
Hind Swaraj was written in 1909 on the ship Kildonan Castle.
My Experiments with Truth was serialised in Navajivan.
Nai Talim (Wardha Scheme, 1937) was framed by a committee under Zakir Hussain.
Henry David Thoreau's essay "Civil Disobedience" influenced Gandhi's idea of resisting unjust laws.

items.title: Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda — Detail
items.body:
### Champaran, Ahmedabad and Kheda — Detail

**In one line**
The people, numbers and results of Gandhi's three first Indian campaigns, and his other positions of 1916–18.

**The story**
Gandhi first spoke out at the opening of **Banaras Hindu University** (1916). In 1917 **Rajkumar Shukla** brought him to Champaran, where planters, losing money to **German** synthetic dyes, forced peasants into **tinkathia** — indigo on **3 of every 20** kathas. Gandhi ignored an order to leave, was tried at **Motihari**, and with **Rajendra Prasad**, **Mazharul Haq**, **Narhari Parikh** and others collected peasant evidence; as a member of the **Champaran Agrarian** Committee he won the 1918 Act. At Ahmedabad the **plague bonus** dispute ended in a **35%** award after his **first hunger strike**, with **Anasuya Sarabhai** opposing her brother **Ambalal**. In Kheda the rules gave remission if the crop fell below **25%**; Gandhi, **Patel**, **Indulal Yagnik** and **Mohanlal Pandya** led a no-revenue campaign. In the same year he recruited for the army at the **War Conference** — and his long campaign ended **indentured** emigration (1917).

#### 1916–1918

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Invitation** | **Rajkumar Shukla** brought Gandhi to Champaran |
| **Tinkathia** | Indigo on **3 of every 20** kathas (3/20 of a bigha) |
| **Why planters squeezed** | Synthetic **German** dyes; planters raised rents (sharahbeshi) to release peasants |
| **Defiance** | Disobeyed an order to leave; case at **Motihari** dropped |
| **Result** | Gandhi on the **Champaran Agrarian** Committee → Champaran Agrarian Act **1918**; 25% of illegal dues refunded |
| **Champaran team** | Rajendra Prasad, **Mazharul Haq**, Kripalani, Mahadev Desai, **Narhari Parikh**, Anugrah Narayan Sinha |
| **Ahmedabad mill strike** | **Plague bonus** withdrawn; demand 50%, offer 20%, award **35**% |
| **Anasuya Sarabhai** | Sister of mill-owner **Ambalal** Sarabhai; sided with the workers |
| **Union** | Textile Labour Association — **Majoor Mahajan** Sangh (1920) |
| **First fast** | Gandhi's **first hunger strike** in India |
| **Kheda rule** | Remission due if yield < **25%** of normal; harvest failed 1917–18 |
| **Kheda team** | Vallabhbhai Patel, **Indulal Yagnik**, **Mohanlal Pandya** ("Dungli chor"); Gujarat Sabha |
| **Tags** | Champaran = first civil disobedience; Kheda = **first non-cooperation** |
| **War Conference** | Delhi, April 1918 (Chelmsford); Gandhi backed recruitment — "**recruiting sergeant**" |
| **Indenture** | Campaign against **indentured** emigration — ended **1917** |
| **BHU speech** | Opening of **Banaras Hindu University**, Feb **1916** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Champaran** = first **civil disobedience** (Bihar, indigo); **Ahmedabad** = first **hunger strike** (mill bonus); **Kheda** = first **non-cooperation** (revenue).
- At the 1918 War Conference Gandhi **supported** recruitment — a trap in UPSC 2019.

**TL;DR**
- Champaran 1917: Rajkumar Shukla; tinkathia 3/20; Motihari; Agrarian Act 1918.
- Ahmedabad 1918: plague bonus, 35% award; first hunger strike; Anasuya Sarabhai.
- Kheda 1918: remission rule <25%; Patel, Indulal Yagnik, Mohanlal Pandya.
- War Conference 1918: recruiting; indentured emigration ended 1917.
keyPoints: Rajkumar Shukla brought Gandhi to Champaran.
Tinkathia forced indigo on 3 of every 20 kathas.
At Ahmedabad the tribunal awarded a 35% bonus.
At the 1918 War Conference Gandhi supported army recruitment.

items.title: Gandhi from Rowlatt to Belgaum (1919–1925)
items.body:
### Gandhi from Rowlatt to Belgaum (1919–1925)

**In one line**
Gandhi's own steps in 1919–25: the Satyagraha Sabha, the Khilafat alliance, the Non-Cooperation programme, prison and constructive work.

**The story**
Against the Rowlatt Bills Gandhi formed the **Satyagraha Sabha** (February 1919); he was arrested at **Palwal** on the way to Punjab and, when violence broke out, called the launch a '**Himalayan miscalculation**'. The Treaty of **Sèvres** (1920) turned Muslim anger into the Khilafat movement, whose conference he had chaired in 1919. Returning his **Kaiser-i-Hind** medal, he launched Non-Cooperation on **three demands** — the **Punjab wrongs**, the Khilafat wrong and **Swaraj** — promising Swaraj within **one year**; he also took over the Home Rule League as the **Swarajya Sabha**. After Chauri Chaura came the **Great Trial** (1922) and jail until **February 1924**. Free again, he fasted for unity (**September 1924**), presided at Belgaum and set up the **All India Spinners' Association** (1925).

#### 1919–1925

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Satyagraha Sabha** | Bombay, **February 1919**; pledge against the Rowlatt Bills |
| **Arrest** | At **Palwal**, 9 April 1919, on the way to Punjab |
| **Self-criticism** | '**Himalayan miscalculation**' — suspended the Rowlatt satyagraha after violence (April 1919) |
| **Khilafat grievance** | Treaty of **Sèvres** (1920) dismembered the Ottoman empire |
| **Khilafat Conference** | Delhi, Nov 1919 — Gandhi presided |
| **Titles returned** | Gandhi returned the **Kaiser-i-Hind** medal (1920) |
| **Three demands** | **Punjab wrongs**, Khilafat wrong, **Swaraj** |
| **Promise** | 'Swaraj within **one year**' |
| **Home Rule League** | Gandhi president (1920); renamed **Swarajya Sabha** |
| **Great Trial** | Ahmedabad, March 1922; 6 years; released **February 1924** (appendicitis) |
| **1924 fast** | 21 days, Delhi, **September 1924**, for **Hindu–Muslim unity** |
| **Khadi body** | **All India Spinners' Association**, **1925** |

**Don't confuse**
- **Himalayan miscalculation** (1919, Rowlatt violence) ≠ the **Chauri Chaura** withdrawal (1922).
- **Satyagraha Sabha** (1919, Rowlatt) ≠ **Swarajya Sabha** (1920, renamed Home Rule League).

**TL;DR**
- Satyagraha Sabha Feb 1919; Palwal arrest; "Himalayan miscalculation".
- Sèvres 1920; Khilafat Conference 1919 (Gandhi presided); Kaiser-i-Hind returned.
- NCM demands: Punjab, Khilafat, Swaraj; "Swaraj in one year"; Swarajya Sabha.
- Great Trial 1922 → released Feb 1924; unity fast Sept 1924; AISA 1925.
keyPoints: Gandhi set up the Satyagraha Sabha in February 1919.
Gandhi called the 1919 launch a 'Himalayan miscalculation'.
The Treaty of Sèvres provoked the Khilafat movement.
Gandhi founded the All India Spinners' Association in 1925.

items.title: Gandhi and Civil Disobedience (1930–1934) — Detail
items.body:
### Gandhi and Civil Disobedience (1930–1934) — Detail

**In one line**
Gandhi's own steps in the salt satyagraha, the Delhi Pact, London, the epic fast and the Harijan campaign.

**The story**
Gandhi's **Eleven Points** (Young India, **31 January 1930**) were ignored, so he marched about 385 km in **24 days** to the **Navsari** coast. Arrested at **Karadi** in May 1930, he talked in prison with **Sapru** and **Jayakar**. The **Gandhi–Irwin Pact** withdrew the **ordinances**, freed non-violent **prisoners** and allowed salt-making on the **coast** and peaceful **picketing** — but not an inquiry into **police excesses** or a reprieve for **Bhagat Singh**. Gandhi sailed on the **SS Rajputana**, stayed at **Kingsley Hall**, and drew Churchill's '**half-naked fakir**' jibe. Back in jail, he fasted at **Yerawada** from **20 September 1932** against the Communal Award, then founded the **Anti-Untouchability League** (soon the **Harijan Sevak Sangh**), toured India for Harijans and in **October 1934** **resigned** from the Congress for constructive work.

#### 1930–1934

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Ultimatum** | **Eleven Points**, Young India, **31 January 1930** |
| **Dandi** | **Navsari** coast, Gujarat; ~385 km (240 mi) in **24 days** |
| **Arrest** | **Karadi**, night of 4–5 May 1930 → Yerawada |
| **Mediators** | Tej Bahadur Sapru & M.R. **Jayakar** (1930) |
| **Pact — govt gave** | Withdraw **ordinances** & prosecutions; release non-violent **prisoners**; return confiscated land not sold |
| **Pact — salt** | Salt for personal use on the **coast**; peaceful **picketing** allowed |
| **Pact — refused** | NO inquiry into **police excesses**; NO commutation for **Bhagat Singh** |
| **London 1931** | Sailed on **SS Rajputana**; stayed at **Kingsley Hall**, East End |
| **Churchill** | '**Half-naked fakir**' (1931) |
| **Epic fast** | **Yerawada** jail, from **20 September 1932** |
| **Harijan work** | **All India Anti-Untouchability League** (Sept 1932) → renamed **Harijan Sevak Sangh** |
| **Harijan tour** | Nov 1933 – July 1934, all India |
| **Resignation** | **Resigned** Congress membership, **October 1934** |
| **Village industries** | **All India Village Industries Association** (1934) |

**Don't confuse**
- The Pact gave **coastal salt for personal use**, not abolition of the salt tax.
- **Anti-Untouchability League** (1932) was renamed **Harijan Sevak Sangh**; the paper **Harijan** began in 1933.

**TL;DR**
- Eleven Points 31 Jan 1930; Dandi ~385 km in 24 days; arrest at Karadi.
- Pact gave: ordinances withdrawn, prisoners freed, coastal salt, picketing; NOT police-excess inquiry, NOT Bhagat Singh reprieve.
- London: SS Rajputana, Kingsley Hall, 'half-naked fakir'.
- Yerawada fast 20 Sept 1932; Anti-Untouchability League → Harijan Sevak Sangh; resigned Congress Oct 1934.
keyPoints: The Gandhi–Irwin Pact allowed coastal people to make salt for their own use.
The Pact did not grant an inquiry into police excesses.
Churchill called Gandhi a 'half-naked fakir'.
Gandhi resigned from the Congress in October 1934.

items.title: Gandhi's Last Years (1939–1948) and His Titles
items.body:
### Gandhi's Last Years (1939–1948) and His Titles

**In one line**
From Individual Satyagraha to the bullet at Birla House — the facts of Gandhi's final decade, and the names others gave him.

**The story**
In 1940 Gandhi chose **Vinoba Bhave** as the **first individual satyagrahi**, and in January 1942 named Nehru his **political heir**. His Quit India speech gave orders to every group, from **government servants** to **students**. In the **Aga Khan Palace** he lost his secretary **Mahadev Desai** (1942) and his wife **Kasturba** (**22 February 1944**); he was freed on **6 May 1944**. Bose hailed him as '**Father of the Nation**' on **6 July 1944**. When riots came he walked through **Noakhali**, spent **15 August 1947** fasting in **Calcutta** — a '**one-man boundary force**' — and fasted a last time (**13–18 January 1948**) for peace and Pakistan's **₹55 crore**. Godse shot him at **Birla House** on **30 January 1948**; Godse and **Narayan Apte** were hanged in 1949. His samadhi is at **Raj Ghat**, and the UN keeps 2 October as the **International Day of Non-Violence**.

#### 1940–1948

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Individual Satyagraha** | Vinoba Bhave the **first individual satyagrahi** (Oct 1940), Nehru second |
| **Heir** | Nehru named his **political heir** (Wardha, Jan 1942) |
| **8 August 1942 speech** | "Do or Die"; instructions to **government servants**, soldiers, princes, peasants, **students** |
| **Mahadev Desai** | Gandhi's secretary; died at the Aga Khan Palace, Aug 1942 |
| **Kasturba** | Died at the Aga Khan Palace, **22 February 1944** |
| **Release** | **6 May 1944** — last imprisonment ended |
| **"Father of the Nation"** | Subhas Bose, radio address, **6 July 1944** |
| **Noakhali** | Peace march, Nov 1946 – Mar 1947, East Bengal |
| **Calcutta 1947** | Fast stopped riots; Mountbatten: '**one-man boundary force**' |
| **Independence Day** | On **15 August 1947** Gandhi was in **Calcutta** (Beliaghata), not Delhi |
| **Last fast** | **13–18 January 1948**, Delhi — peace and the ₹**55 crore** due to Pakistan |
| **Assassination** | **Birla House**, **30 January 1948**, evening prayer; last words "He Ram" (traditional) |
| **Trial** | Godse & **Narayan Apte** hanged Nov 1949 (Red Fort trial) |
| **Memorial** | Samadhi at **Raj Ghat**; 30 Jan = **Martyrs' Day**; 2 Oct = International Day of Non-Violence |
| **UN** | 2 October = **International Day of Non-Violence** (UN, **2007**) |

#### Titles and names

| Title | Who / whom |
|---|---|
| **'Mahatma'** | Credited to Rabindranath **Tagore** |
| **'Gurudev'** | Gandhi's name for Tagore |
| **'Bapu'** | Popular name — father |
| **'Conscience keeper'** | Gandhi's description of **C. Rajagopalachari** |
| **'Deenabandhu'** | **C.F. Andrews**, Gandhi's friend |

**Don't confuse**
- '**Mahatma**' (Tagore gave it to Gandhi) vs '**Gurudev**' (Gandhi gave it to Tagore).
- '**Father of the Nation**' — Bose, 1944; '**Half-naked fakir**' — Churchill, 1931; '**One-man boundary force**' — Mountbatten, 1947.

**TL;DR**
- Vinoba first individual satyagrahi 1940; Nehru political heir 1942.
- Aga Khan Palace: Mahadev Desai died 1942, Kasturba 22 Feb 1944; released 6 May 1944.
- Bose: Father of the Nation, 6 July 1944; Noakhali 1946–47; Calcutta 15 Aug 1947.
- Last fast 13–18 Jan 1948; Birla House 30 Jan 1948; Raj Ghat; UN Day of Non-Violence 2007.
keyPoints: Subhas Bose called Gandhi 'Father of the Nation' on 6 July 1944.
Kasturba died at the Aga Khan Palace on 22 February 1944.
On 15 August 1947 Gandhi was in Calcutta.
Gandhi was shot at Birla House on 30 January 1948.
Gandhi called Tagore 'Gurudev'.

items.title: Gandhi and Andhra — Visits, Flag and Khadi
items.body:
### Gandhi and Andhra — Visits, Flag and Khadi

**In one line**
Andhra was one of the most Gandhian regions of the south: the 1921 Bezawada AICC, the national flag, the khadi tours and the local satyagrahas.

**The story**
The Congress's first big Non-Cooperation meeting in the south was the AICC at **Bezawada** (Vijayawada) on 31 March–1 April **1921**, which fixed the targets of ₹1 crore, a crore members and 20 lakh charkhas. There **Pingali Venkayya** of Machilipatnam showed Gandhi a red-and-green flag; a white band was added at Gandhi's suggestion and a **charkha** placed on it — the ancestor of today's tricolour. That year Gandhi backed the **Duggirala** Gopalakrishnayya exodus at Chirala–Perala, and in 1930 **Bulusu Sambamurthy** made salt at **Chollangi** near Kakinada. Gandhi returned in **1929** on a **khadi** fund tour, praising the fine cloth of **Ponduru** in Srikakulam, and again in **December 1933** for Harijan work.

#### Gandhi and Andhra

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Bezawada AICC** | Vijayawada, 31 Mar – 1 Apr **1921**; ₹1 crore Tilak Swaraj Fund, 1 crore members, 20 lakh charkhas |
| **Flag** | **Pingali Venkayya** showed a red-green flag at Bezawada; white stripe added at Gandhi's suggestion; a **charkha** at the centre (Lala Hansraj's idea) |
| **Khadi tour** | Andhra tour, April–May **1929**, for **khadi** funds |
| **Harijan tour** | Andhra districts, **December 1933** |
| **Ponduru khadi** | **Ponduru** (Srikakulam) — fine hand-spun khadi praised by Gandhi |
| **Chirala–Perala** | Gandhi encouraged **Duggirala** Gopalakrishnayya's town exodus (1921) |
| **Chollangi** | Salt Satyagraha near Kakinada — **Bulusu Sambamurthy** arrested 18 April 1930 |

**Don't confuse**
- **Bezawada AICC (1921)** ≠ **Kakinada Congress session (1923)** — the first was a committee meeting, the second a full annual session.
- Pingali Venkayya's design was **adapted**; the Constituent Assembly adopted the present flag on 22 July 1947 with the **Ashoka chakra** in place of the charkha.

**TL;DR**
- Bezawada AICC 31 Mar–1 Apr 1921: ₹1 crore, 1 crore members, 20 lakh charkhas.
- Pingali Venkayya showed Gandhi a flag at Bezawada.
- Khadi tour 1929 (Ponduru khadi praised); Harijan tour Dec 1933.
- Chirala–Perala 1921 (Duggirala); Salt Satyagraha at Chollangi (Bulusu Sambamurthy, 1930).
keyPoints: The AICC met at Bezawada (Vijayawada) in 1921.
Pingali Venkayya presented a flag design to Gandhi at Bezawada.
Gandhi toured Andhra for khadi in 1929.
Gandhi praised the khadi of Ponduru in Srikakulam.

items.title: Gandhi's Satyagrahas and Fasts at a Glance
items.body:
### Gandhi's Satyagrahas and Fasts at a Glance

**In one line**
One table for the places and years of the Gandhian satyagrahas, including the temple-entry and local campaigns, and one for his major fasts.

**The story**
Besides the three famous national movements, Gandhi's method spread to many local satyagrahas. **Champaran** (Bihar) and **Kheda** (Gujarat) came first; in the 1920s came the **Flag Satyagraha** at **Nagpur**, Patel's **Borsad** campaign and the **Vaikom** struggle in Travancore led by **T.K. Madhavan**, which Gandhi visited; in 1931–32 **K. Kelappan** fasted at **Guruvayur** for temple entry. Gandhi's own weapon of last resort was the fast — for the **mill-workers** (1918), against separate seats for the **Depressed Classes** (1932), for **self-purification** (May 1933), at **Rajkot** (1939), against the government **blaming** the Congress (February 1943), in Calcutta (**September 1947**) and finally in Delhi (January 1948).

#### Satyagrahas

| Satyagraha | Year | Place | Issue / leaders |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Champaran** | 1917 | **Bihar** (West Champaran) | Indigo / tinkathia |
| **Kheda** | 1918 | **Gujarat** (Kaira) | Land revenue remission |
| **Vaikom** | 1924–25 | Travancore (Kerala) | Temple-road access; **T.K. Madhavan**, K.P. Kesava Menon; Gandhi visited 1925 |
| **Guruvayur** | 1931–32 | Malabar (Kerala) | Temple entry; **K. Kelappan** fasted |
| **Borsad** | 1923–24 | Gujarat | Punitive "dacoity tax"; led by Patel |
| **Flag Satyagraha** | 1923 | **Nagpur** (also Jabalpur) | Right to carry the national flag; Jamnalal Bajaj, Patel |
| **Rajkot** | 1939 | Rajkot princely state | Gandhi fasted (March **1939**) for promised reforms |

#### Major fasts

| Fast | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **1918 Ahmedabad** | For the **mill-workers** (3 days) |
| **1932 Yerawada** | Against separate electorates for the **Depressed Classes** |
| **May 1933** | 21-day **self-purification** fast (Harijan cause) |
| **Feb 1943** | 21 days, Aga Khan Palace — against the government **blaming** Congress for 1942 violence |
| **Sept 1947** | Calcutta — stopped the riots |

**Don't confuse**
- **Vaikom** (1924–25, temple roads, T.K. Madhavan) ≠ **Guruvayur** (1931–32, temple entry, K. Kelappan).
- **Borsad** (1923–24) and **Bardoli** (1928) were both Patel's Gujarat campaigns.

**TL;DR**
- Champaran 1917 Bihar; Kheda 1918 Gujarat; Flag Satyagraha Nagpur 1923; Borsad 1923–24.
- Vaikom 1924–25 (T.K. Madhavan); Guruvayur 1931–32 (K. Kelappan); Rajkot 1939.
- Fasts: 1918 mill-workers; 1924 unity; 1932 Depressed Classes; 1933 self-purification; 1943; Sept 1947 Calcutta; Jan 1948 Delhi.
keyPoints: The Vaikom Satyagraha (1924–25) was led by T.K. Madhavan and K.P. Kesava Menon.
K. Kelappan led the Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931–32).
The Flag Satyagraha of 1923 was centred at Nagpur.
Gandhi's 1932 Yerawada fast was against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes.

items.title: For Mains — Gandhi: Thoughts & Satyagrahas
items.body:
### For Mains — assessing the Gandhian era

**In one line**
For Mains, treat Gandhi as a method and a philosophy to be evaluated — weigh what Satyagraha achieved, what it could not, and how it shaped India after 1947.

**Why it is asked**
APPSC Paper-2 (Indian history and national movement) asks you to analyse Gandhian techniques, assess the mass movements and critically examine his social thought — not just narrate events.

**The dimensions Mains asks**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Philosophy | Truth, Ahimsa, Satyagraha, means-ends unity (Hind Swaraj), trusteeship |
| Technique | Non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting, constructive programme |
| Mass base | Drew in peasants, workers, women and the depressed classes for the first time |
| Achievements | Made nationalism a mass force; moral delegitimising of the Raj |
| Criticism/limits | Chauri Chaura withdrawal, Khilafat's communal after-effects, Ambedkar's critique of Harijan paternalism |
| Relevance / way forward | Non-violent protest, trusteeship and ethics in public life today |

**Data points / reports / judgments to quote**
- **Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad and Kheda (1918)** — the three experiments that proved the method.
- **Hind Swaraj (1909)** — the text for means-ends unity and the critique of modern civilisation.
- **Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931)** and the **Second Round Table Conference** — negotiation as a tool.
- **Poona Pact (1932)** with Ambedkar — reserved seats versus separate electorates; cite the Ambedkar debate.
- **Quit India (1942), 'Do or Die'** — the final mass push.

**The AP angle**
Andhra answered every Gandhian call: **Tanguturi Prakasam ('Andhra Kesari')**, Konda Venkatappayya and Pattabhi Sitaramayya led Congress work, and the banned songs of poet **Garimella Satyanarayana** show how Gandhian nationalism took regional, cultural form.

**Use in answers**
- Example to cite: the Chauri Chaura withdrawal to argue that for Gandhi non-violence was a principle, not a tactic.
- A quote: Gandhi's own 'means are after all everything... as the means so the end' for the ethics dimension.
- A diagram idea: a flow from South Africa → three early Satyagrahas → three mass movements, with 'constructive programme' as a parallel band.
keyPoints: Frame Gandhi as philosophy + technique: Truth/Ahimsa/Satyagraha, means-ends unity, trusteeship, constructive programme.
Show the widening mass base: peasants, workers, women and the depressed classes enter politics.
Assess achievements (mass nationalism, moral delegitimising of the Raj) against limits (Chauri Chaura, Khilafat's communal fallout, Ambedkar's critique).
Quote Champaran/Ahmedabad/Kheda (1917-18), Hind Swaraj (1909), Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931), Poona Pact (1932), Quit India (1942).
AP angle: Prakasam, Konda Venkatappayya, Pattabhi Sitaramayya and poet Garimella Satyanarayana carried Gandhian nationalism in Andhra.
Relevance: non-violent protest, trusteeship and ethics in public life remain live themes.
